entries.author: siyuanfeng636-cpu
entries.license_notes: Depends on HeyGen's HyperFrames CLI (separate project/terms) and optional paid TTS (OpenAI, ElevenLabs).
entries.hook: A skill that turns a URL, paper or proposal into a GSAP motion video — Whisper word timing, synthesized 120 BPM score, HyperFrames render.
entries.source: GitHub guide (opus_motion_video_guide.md)
entries.body:
## What it is

An agent skill (`SKILL.md` + helper scripts + prompt templates + a boilerplate project) for making commercial motion videos without a video editor. The README is part English, part Chinese. It was inspired by Moritz Kremb's "Opus 5.5 solved motion graphics" workflow.

## How it works

Six steps:

1. **Research:** read the source. For a reference video, `scripts/contact_sheet.py` makes a frame grid the model can "watch".
2. **Script:** write `scripts/script.json` with each scene's narration, on-screen text, layout and SFX cues.
3. **Voiceover:** `scripts/tts_engine.py` (OpenAI `tts-1-hd` / `gpt-4o-mini-tts` or ElevenLabs), then ffmpeg trims silences and speeds up 1.05–1.1×.
4. **Alignment:** `scripts/timing_aligner.py` (whisper.cpp / faster-whisper) writes word-level `timing.json`.
5. **Build:** `index.html` with GSAP timelines bound to `timing.json`; `scripts/synth_sfx.py` synthesizes a 120 BPM music bed and UI sounds with numpy/scipy.
6. **Check and render:** `npx hyperframes lint`, `npx hyperframes snapshot --time 1.0,2.5,4.0` (for visual self-review), `npx hyperframes render`, then ffmpeg normalizes to −14 LUFS.

It covers five archetypes with prompt templates: SaaS product launch, article/paper explainer cartoon, longform→vertical shortform, personalized client proposal video, and animated presentation.

## Ideas for us

- **Personalized proposal video** is a direct fit for CTX pitches: a client's brand plus our installation concept, animated with milestones.
- The `script.json` schema plus word-level `timing.json` is a clean contract worth copying for our own reel template.
- Synthesized SFX on a BPM grid pairs with our `_shared/sound.ts` procedural audio approach.

## Notes

- Verified 2026-10-03 (README, SKILL.md, file tree). The guide's summary is accurate.
- It is installed as `~/.agents/skills/agentic-motion-graphics` (the Antigravity convention). For Claude Code, copy it to `~/.claude/skills/` instead.
- Very new (created 2026-09-25), and the scripts haven't been run by us.

entries.title: animation-pipeline — code-made music videos in riso cut-paper style
entries.author: bishpls
entries.license_notes: No LICENSE file. Third film is an unofficial Clawd fan work.
entries.hook: Films where a WebGL shader prints every frame as mid-century cut paper on four riso inks — misregistration, halftones, paper grain.
entries.source: GitHub search for paper-cut animation, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

A base for making films with Claude Code, with three finished works.
- *OPEN ALL NIGHT*: a 93 s cut-paper title sequence in the style of Saul Bass / *Catch Me If You Can*, on four riso inks.
- *WORDS ARE FOSSILS*: 86 s vertical, letterpress look.
- *HELLO, WORLD!*: a J-pop style piece.

## How it works

- **Picture:** riso simulation in a shader. Blue, fluorescent pink, yellow and black inks with overprint multiply, halftone tints, misregistration, ink mottling and paper grain. "Light is paper": lit windows and neon are knockouts.
- **Type:** variable-font glyph outlines (fontkit) animated per glyph.
- **Sound:** sign clicks and hum are synthesised from the same schedule the picture draws.
- **Song:** ElevenLabs Music. The best of seven takes was chosen by beat-grid fit, seam analysis, speech-to-text intelligibility and blind Gemini rankings (Borda count). Word timestamps print lyrics on their sung syllable.
- **Process:** storyboard → slate animatic → five parallel sub-agents against one craft guide → review passes (contact sheets, strips, crops, seam checks).

## Ideas for us

- The riso overprint shader is a strong, cheap house look for event posters that animate into reels.

## Notes

README read 2026-10-03.

entries.title: Box2D — 2D physics engine for games
entries.author: Erin Catto
entries.license_notes: Reel added its own pyramid + 20-level scene and paper-texture rendering on top.
entries.hook: The 2D physics engine for games — things fall, stack and crash, with very stable piles.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

The classic 2D rigid-body engine (behind Angry Birds, Limbo and countless others). Version 3 is a C rewrite with a "soft step" solver, SIMD and multithreading, so it can run very large stacks and piles stably.

## How it works

- Broad phase (dynamic AABB tree), then narrow-phase contact manifolds, then a constraint solver for contacts and joints (revolute, prismatic, weld, mouse, ...).
- v3's soft-step solver uses sub-stepping plus soft constraints, which keeps tall pyramids standing and avoids jitter.
- Bodies sleep when at rest, so big scenes stay cheap.

## Ideas for us

- **digital-doodles-wall:** submitted doodles become physical bodies that rain down, pile up and get knocked over.
- **avatar-arcade:** tracked silhouettes or hands as kinematic bodies batting objects around.
- **rhythm-battle:** each team's energy spawns blocks; the taller tower wins.

## Notes

Web: box2d3 WASM builds, or Planck.js (pure-JS v2 port). Matter.js is simpler but less stable for big stacks.

## What it is

A Claude Code / Claude.ai skill that turns a myth or premise into a finished narrated short film. The look: flat matte cardstock worlds with visible cut edges and soft contact shadows, a strict three-colour palette, a tiny figure centred in a huge symmetrical set, a top-down concentric "ring" hero shot, and paper-wipe transitions.

2. Lore research on the real tradition.

entries.body:
## What it is

A physically simulated oil-painting studio for AI painters. The `paint` crate models a primed linen canvas, a bristle brush that carries wet paint, paint that levels and dries on a clock, cracks, and layers combined optically with Kubelka–Munk. Colours come only from piles mixed with a palette knife from named tubes. The `easel` crate is a live Lua session over that engine, which Claude uses to paint like a painter: mix, load, stroke, wait for layers to dry. Finished works and live studios are shown at stillwet.art.

## How it works

- **Optics, not RGB:** each pigment has absorption and scattering coefficients, and Kubelka–Munk theory computes how mixed and layered paint reflects light. That's why mixes go muddy or glow the way real oils do (blue + yellow really makes green).
- **Bristles:** a brush is many simulated bristles depositing and picking up wet paint, so strokes have ridges, drag and smear.
- **Time:** paint dries on a clock, so painting wet-on-wet versus waiting changes the result.
- **Paintings are replayable logs:** every painting is a log of easel commands, and renders are regenerated rather than stored. Paintings are run in "rounds", with a studio viewer showing painters working live or replayed.

```sh
cargo build --release -p easel
cargo test --workspace
```
Read `notes/easel_guide.md` (how to paint) and `notes/research/` (sourced notes on paint physics).

## Ideas for us

- **mural-wall / synesthetic-room:** a live "the room is painting" installation, where crowd input decides what Claude paints next and the canvas dries over the evening.
- **merch-takeaway:** a print of the night's painting, with its replayable stroke log as a timelapse reel.
- Kubelka–Munk mixing is the trick to steal for any digital paint effect (it is also used in the Mixbox pigment library).

## Notes

README read 2026-10-03. The README carries a "keep out of training data" benchmark canary, so treat the repo as reference material. Paintings and logs are CC BY 4.0: credit "alice / stillwet.art" if shown.

entries.body:
## What it is

A small starter kit for animating a hand-painted character with p5.js + p5.brush and Claude Opus 5.5. It is built from the PDoomVideo code plus the author's analysis of what the model did well and badly. It includes the Clawd character (views, 31 acted emotions, eyes, mouths, hats, emotes, dances) and a guide the model reads before animating.

## How it works

Open the repo in Claude Code and ask, e.g. *"Read ANIMATION_GUIDE.md, then make a 15-second video of Clawd trying to catch a butterfly."* The model then:

1. Storyboards first.
2. Builds shot by shot.
3. Renders contact sheets to check its own work.
4. Writes `out/video.mp4`.

The guide's rules include: handmade, alive, one piece, no text, always transitions, something happens in every scene, and a consistent medium of brush strokes, flat 2D and boiling linework.

- `src/core.js`: painting, timing, motion helpers, camera, light, paper.
- `src/timeline.js`: shots, loops and the brush-wipe transition.
- `src/config.js`: length and tempo.
- `src/scenes/`: your video goes here.
- `render.mjs`: contact sheets, frame strips, crops, stills and MP4.

```bash
npm install
node render.mjs --clip --out=out/video.mp4     # renders the 11 s demo
```

Open `studio.html` in Chrome to scrub; add `?loop=emotions` or `?loop=views` to see the model sheets.

## Ideas for us

- Fork it as the base for a CTX "reel kit": replace Clawd with our own character or brand mark, and keep the timeline, contact-sheet and render tooling.
- The author's tip: higher reasoning effort makes scenes more extravagant and detailed (the test videos used xhigh).

## Notes

- Without a dedicated GPU, p5.brush watercolour fills render at seconds per frame. Ask the model to avoid them on integrated graphics.
- Linux flags: `--soft-gl` (no GPU), `--gpu-angle=gl-egl` or `vulkan` (headless NVIDIA); `node gpu_probe.mjs` shows which renderer you get.
- Verified 2026-10-03 against the README and file tree.

entries.body:
## What it is

A guide to making motion videos where the model writes **animation code** (HTML + Canvas/SVG/JS, often p5.js or GSAP), a headless browser renders it frame by frame, and ffmpeg encodes the result. Because it is deterministic code rather than diffusion, characters and brand elements stay identical from frame 1 to frame 500.

## How it works

```
brief → treatment/storyboard → animation code → headless Chrome seeks frame i (t = i/fps)
→ screenshot each frame → ffmpeg stitches frames + audio → .mp4
```

**Core rule:** the whole film is a pure function of time with no hidden state:

```js
function draw(ctx, t) { /* draw exactly what is on screen at t seconds */ }
window.seek = (t) => draw(ctx, t);
```

That makes rendering **parallel** (N Chrome workers), **resumable**, and frame-exact.

```bash
node render.mjs --frames=0:20 --workers=4      # render PNG frames
node render.mjs --encode --out=out/final.mp4   # ffmpeg frames + audio
```

**Workflow with Claude Code:**

1. Brief: topic, length, tone, aspect (9:16 Reels/Shorts, 16:9 YouTube).
2. Ask for a **treatment/storyboard first**, approve it, *then* the code.
3. Render a **contact sheet** of test frames before the full render.
4. Iterate with plain-language notes ("slow scene 2").

**Levels:**

- *Zero setup:* ask for a self-contained HTML animation, preview as an artifact, then screen-record it.
- *Local pipeline:* Node ≥ 22, Chrome, Playwright, ffmpeg (+ p5.js / p5.brush / GSAP).
- *Advanced:*
  - Whisper word timestamps and beat/onset analysis so cuts land on audio.
  - Audio from files, `yt-dlp`, Web Audio synthesis, or ElevenLabs/OpenAI TTS.
  - A planner agent writes a style guide while sub-agents build scenes.
  - Self-review of contact sheets.
  - three.js when 3D is needed.
  - WebGL post: grain, chromatic aberration, real motion blur via sub-frame accumulation.
  - QA the encoded MP4 with jankscan.

## Ideas for us

- **reels-content:** promo reels for every installation built from the *same* code as the installation visuals: same palette, same particles, same brand, frame-exact.
- Recreate the @index.opensource reel format (caption band + clips) as a reusable HTML template with `seek(t)`.
- Our installation web clients (Vite/React) could expose a `window.seek` debug mode to render perfect showcase videos.

## Notes

- **Hook line from the guide:** "AI video didn't get better — it stopped being AI video."
- Requirements recap: Claude Code + Opus, Node ≥ 22, Chrome/Chromium, ffmpeg, Python 3 + numpy, `yt-dlp`, optional `openai-whisper`.
- Shared via a link with tracking params; canonical URL above.
- **Corrections after checking every linked repo (2026-10-03):**
  - PDoomVideo has no license; the guide calls it "MIT-adjacent".
  - Motion Reel ’26 (SuhaasNv) and shipvideo also have no license, so they are reference-only.
  - shipvideo keeps videos in the OpenComputer workspace, not Vercel Blob.
  - jankscan's own benchmark catches only 47% of dropped frames and flags 25 of 40 clean videos.
  - DistilBook pricing has changed (now 10 free credits, $20/$50/$100 plans).
  - Everything else matched.

entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

`d3-delaunay` computes the Delaunay triangulation of a point set and its dual, the Voronoi diagram, very fast. It is built on **Delaunator** (Mapbox), which uses **robust-predicates** for exact orientation tests so degenerate inputs don't break it.

## How it works

- `Delaunay.from(points)` → triangles; `.voronoi([x0, y0, x1, y1])` → clipped cells.
- `cellPolygon(i)` / `cellPolygons()` for drawing; `delaunay.find(x, y)` gives the nearest site in roughly O(1) when walking from the last result, which makes hover and hit-testing cheap.
- **Weighted Voronoi stippling** (Adrian Secord, 2002): scatter points, compute Voronoi, move each point to its cell's centroid *weighted by image darkness*, repeat (Lloyd relaxation). Points crowd into dark areas, which gives a stipple drawing of the image. The reel shows "iteration 31" of this converging.

## Ideas for us

- **memory-mosaic:** organic Voronoi cells instead of a square grid; each guest face clipped to a cell, sites relaxed towards the target image's darkness so the mosaic *is* a stipple of the target.
- **living-floor:** one site per tracked foot or person, so the cells reshape as people move; cell borders become the light lines.
- **merch-takeaway:** stipple a guest's selfie and pen-plot it (pipe through vpype).
- Cheap nearest-neighbour lookup for any interaction (which particle or tile is under the finger).

## Notes

- Secord 2002 paper: https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/imager/tr/2002/secord2002b/

sections.What it is: `d3-delaunay` computes the Delaunay triangulation of a point set and its dual, the Voronoi diagram, very fast. It is built on **Delaunator** (Mapbox), which uses **robust-predicates** for exact orientation tests so degenerate inputs don't break it.
sections.How it works:
- `Delaunay.from(points)` → triangles; `.voronoi([x0, y0, x1, y1])` → clipped cells.

Points crowd into dark areas, which gives a stipple drawing of the image. The reel shows "iteration 31" of this converging.

- **memory-mosaic:** organic Voronoi cells instead of a square grid; each guest face clipped to a cell, sites relaxed towards the target image's darkness so the mosaic *is* a stipple of the target.

- **merch-takeaway:** stipple a guest's selfie and pen-plot it (pipe through vpype).
- Cheap nearest-neighbour lookup for any interaction (which particle or tile is under the finger).

entries.title: Differential Line — growing, folding curves
entries.author: Anders Hoff (inconvergent)
entries.license_notes: Code MIT. The author's imagery/GIFs/site footage have separate, unconfirmed reuse terms. Reel simulations rendered by Xity from pinned code.
entries.hook: One closed line keeps growing and folds like a brain or a coral.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

Anders Hoff's classic **differential growth** simulation: a single closed loop of points that keeps lengthening and has to fold to fit, producing brain-coral and lettuce-edge forms.

## How it works

Every step:

1. **Attraction:** each node is pulled towards its two neighbours on the line (keeps it smooth).
2. **Rejection:** each node is pushed away from any other node within radius *r*, found with a spatial hash grid (stops self-intersection).
3. **Growth:** insert new nodes by splitting edges, either at random or weighted by curvature. The reel compares the two side by side; curvature priority gives more even folding.

Starting from an open line or an arc instead of a circle gives different families of shapes.

## Ideas for us

- **collective-heartbeat:** each new heartbeat that joins inserts nodes, so the room's shared line visibly grows all night.
- **merch-takeaway:** plot the final loop. It is a single continuous line, which is perfect for pens.
- **mural-wall:** seed the loop from a guest's drawn outline.

## Notes

Simple to port to JS or GLSL (spatial hash + three forces). Watch the O(n) growth and cap node counts for real-time.

## What it is

Lingdong Huang's generator for imaginary fish in the style of old natural-history engravings. It outputs polylines (SVG, or a plotter-friendly format) from a random seed, so the same seed gives the same fish.

## How it works

- Fish anatomy is parameterised (body outline curve, fins, tail type, eye, scale and stripe patterns), and each parameter is drawn from a seeded PRNG.
- Every part is constructed as vector strokes, including hatching and scale textures, so there are no pixels anywhere.
- Hidden parts are clipped so overlapping fins read correctly in line art.

- **living-swarm / mural-wall:** every guest gets *their* fish, seeded by their name, which swims into a shared aquarium wall (the post literally asks "what name would you draw?").
- **merch-takeaway:** plot the guest's fish on a postcard with their name as the specimen label.
- Pattern sheets and wallpaper for branded spaces.

## Notes

Same author as shan-shui-inf; both are good references for "seeded procedural illustration" generally.

entries.title: fullik — FABRIK inverse kinematics (JS)
entries.author: lo-th
entries.license_notes: JS port of Caliko (Java, MIT, FedUni). Algorithm from Aristidou & Lasenby 2011.
aliases: Forward And Backward Reaching Inverse Kinematics
entries.hook: Chains of bones that reach for a target — creatures, robot arms and lines that follow your hand.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A JavaScript (three.js) port of the Caliko FABRIK library: 2D and 3D inverse-kinematics chains with joint constraints, multiple connected chains, and fixed or free bases. It lets any chain of segments point its tip at a target without matrices or Jacobians.

## How it works

FABRIK (Aristidou & Lasenby, *Graphical Models* 73(5), 2011) is iterative and purely positional:

1. **Backward pass:** snap the end effector onto the target, then walk back towards the root, placing each joint on the line to the next joint at exactly its bone length.
2. **Forward pass:** pin the root back to its base and walk outwards again, re-applying bone lengths.
3. Repeat until the tip is within tolerance (usually a few iterations). Joint constraints (hinge/cone limits) are applied by projecting each bone back into its allowed range during the passes.

It is cheap enough to run hundreds of chains per frame.

## Ideas for us

- **avatar-arcade:** drive avatar limbs from tracked hand or pose keypoints so arms bend naturally.
- **living-swarm:** creatures with IK tentacles or legs that reach for the nearest visitor.
- "Lines that follow your hand": many short chains rooted on a wall edge, all targeting the tracked hand position (the post's "creatures, robot arms, line drawings that follow a hand").
- TouchDesigner: the algorithm is ~40 lines, so it is easy to port into a Script CHOP or GLSL.

## Notes

- Paper: Aristidou, A. & Lasenby, J. (2011) *FABRIK: A fast, iterative solver for the Inverse Kinematics problem*.
- Java original: https://github.com/FedUni/caliko (pin 478786d670f0f1b77461dc1dfc8710b2bc498b2c).

entries.title: Functional Emotions — painted music video with a GPU brushstroke renderer
entries.author: Joshua Ledbetter (directing Claude Opus 5.5)
entries.license_notes: The song, lyrics and audio in assets/ are not covered by the MIT license.
entries.hook: Every frame repainted by about 60,000 instanced GPU brushstrokes that sample an underpainting, follow edges and flow fields, and "boil" like hand-painted animation.
entries.source: Found alongside claude-paint (GitHub search), 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

A 6-minute painted music video made by Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. A first, lyric-video attempt was rejected. Chapter I was directed as the reference, then seven sub-agents painted chapters II–VIII in parallel from `ANIMATION_GUIDE.md`, reviewed on contact sheets. `STORYBOARD.md` has 168 shots.

## How it works

**Renderer (`js/paint.js`):**
- Each shot draws a flat Canvas2D **underpainting** plus an additive **light layer**.
- The GPU repaints the underpainting with about 60k instanced, textured strokes in three size layers. Each stroke samples its colour from beneath and aligns to local edges; in flat areas it follows a flow field.
- Strokes re-roll a few times per second ("boil"), and whip pans smear strokes along the motion.
- The light layer gets bloom, then canvas weave, grain and vignette.

**Timing:**
- Each frame is a pure function of song time.
- A beat grid plus word-level lyric timing drive the cuts.
- Demucs separates the vocals, Whisper transcribes them in chunks, and Needleman–Wunsch alignment matches them to the real lyrics.

```bash
open index.html                               # plays live in the browser
node check.mjs out/sheet.jpg 30 101.5 218.3   # contact sheet at given times
node render.mjs 0 372.7 out/video.mp4 6       # 1080p, 6 parallel pages
```
Use the real GPU (`--use-angle=metal` on macOS). Software GL is about 20× slower. A full render takes about 10 minutes on an M5 Pro.

## Ideas for us

- **Steal the stroke renderer idea for installations:** any live scene (particles, camera feed, guests) as the underpainting, repainted in real time as brushstrokes. That gives a painterly mural-wall or synesthetic-room look at 60 fps.
- The direction notes in the README are a good template for directing Claude on reels: short shots, one action each, the camera always moving, hits on the beat.

## Notes

README read 2026-10-03.

entries.title: GDTF & MVR — open standards for fixtures and whole stage rigs
entries.author: GDTF group (MA Lighting, Robe, Vectorworks + industry); DIN SPEC
entries.license_notes: Spec repo has no LICENSE file; the formats are published as DIN SPEC 15800 (GDTF) and DIN SPEC 15801 (MVR).
entries.hook: One file describes a moving light (GDTF); another describes the whole rig — truss, hoists, fixtures, video, addresses (MVR). Every serious lighting tool reads them.
entries.source: Research for stage design / rigging request, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

- **GDTF** (`.gdtf`, a zip of XML plus 3D models) describes a fixture: geometry, beams, DMX modes and channels, physical data (weight, power).
- **MVR** (`.mvr`) describes a scene: positioned trusses, hoists, fixtures (referencing GDTFs), video screens, scenery, layers and patch.

Together they let a stage design move between CAD (Vectorworks), visualisers (Capture, Depence, grandMA3, Blender DMX), consoles and our own tools without being redrawn.

## How it works

- Fixture files come from **GDTF Share** (manufacturer-uploaded, free account).
- **Libraries:** `pymvr` / `pygdtf` (Python, open-stage), `libMVRgdtf` (C++ reference), and MomentFactory's Omniverse MVR/GDTF→USD converter.
- **MVR-xchange** also defines live sharing of MVR between apps on a network.

## Ideas for us

- Make MVR the single source of truth for event stages. The designer exports MVR → Perastage for review → BlenderDMX for renders → TouchDesigner (td-gdtf) for content previz with the real fixture positions.
- Generate our installation-space MVRs programmatically (pymvr) from venue measurements.

## Notes

Spec repo and BlenderDMX/Perastage READMEs read 2026-10-03.

## What it is

A relighting and glow workflow for After Effects (Windows + macOS) that estimates per-frame depth from plain footage with the **Distill-Any-Depth** model, then uses that depth to place light and glow *in* the scene, not just over it.

## How it works

- A monocular depth model (Distill-Any-Depth) turns each frame into a depth map.
- Inside AE, depth drives light falloff, glow masks and fog, so light can sit between the subject and the background.

## Ideas for us

- **reels-content:** cinematic relit edits of our installation footage (light blooming from the projection onto guests).
- The same idea works live: a monocular depth model on the camera feed in TouchDesigner gives depth-aware projection effects without a depth camera.

## What it is

  - `/faceless-explainer`
  - `/pr-to-video` (from a GitHub PR)
  - `/embedded-captions`
  - `/talking-head-recut`
  - `/motion-graphics` (under 10 s, can be a transparent overlay)
  - `/music-to-video` (beat-synced)

  - `/general-video`

entries.title: jankscan — find stutter in a rendered video before posting
entries.author: stas4000
entries.license_notes: One Python file, standard library plus the ffmpeg binary.
entries.hook: Decodes the actual MP4 (not the source) and flags held, jumped and frozen frames — a CI gate for code-rendered video.
entries.source: GitHub guide (opus_motion_video_guide.md)
entries.body:
## What it is

A QA pass for rendered video. A stuttering file probes as healthy (duration, fps and codec all look fine), so jankscan decodes the frames themselves and reports:

- `held`: a frame repeated while its surroundings move (a dropped render).
- `jump`: a frame that moves about 2× as far as its neighbours (a skipped frame).
- `freeze`: the longest run of repeated frames during motion.

```bash
python3 jankscan.py video.mp4
python3 jankscan.py renders/        # every mp4/mov/webm/mkv in a folder
python3 jankscan.py video.mp4 --json
```

The exit code is 1 when any video stutters, so it works as a CI or render-script gate.

## How it works

ffmpeg decodes every frame to 64×36 grayscale with no frame-rate conversion. For each pair of frames, jankscan takes the mean absolute change and compares it with the median change of the 12 surrounding frames:
- near zero inside steady motion = held;
- 1.6×–2.8× = jump;
- more than that = a cut.

## Ideas for us

- Run it on every exported reel and on TouchDesigner screen captures from installations before posting.

## Notes

The author's own benchmark (40 real videos, one planted fault each) shows real limits. The guide didn't mention them:

- Found the planted **repeated** frame in 26 of 36 (72%).
- Found the planted **dropped** frame in 17 of 36 (47%).
- **Flagged 25 of the 40 untouched videos**: some real stutter, some legitimate jumps like counters or hard cuts.

Treat its output as timestamps to inspect, not a pass/fail verdict. It runs in about 2.6 s per video on one core. Verified 2026-10-03; very new (created 2026-09-25).

entries.author: Michael Fogleman

entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A Go library that renders 3D scenes (spheres, cubes, cylinders, CSG, height functions, triangle meshes/STL) as 2D **polylines** instead of pixels. Hidden lines are removed properly, so the result is a drawing, not a shaded image.

## How it works

- Each shape provides its own set of 3D paths: outlines, latitude/longitude lines, hatching, stripes. For example, a sphere returns lat/long rings and a cube returns its edges or texture stripes.
- Paths are chopped into small segments; each segment's midpoint is ray-cast against the scene to test visibility, and occluded segments are dropped.
- Visible paths are projected with the camera and exported as SVG or PNG.

## Ideas for us

- **merch-takeaway:** a guest's 3D-scanned or avatar mesh rendered as line art and pen-plotted on the spot.
- Monochrome "engraving" look for reels or posters of our installation spaces.
- Combine with **vpype** to optimise plot order and lay out the page.

## Notes

The approach (generate paths per shape → cull by visibility → project) is easy to reproduce in JS with three.js raycasting if we need it in the browser.

entries.body:
## What it is

A desktop app for exploring and rendering 3D fractals: Mandelbulb, Mandelbox, Menger sponge, Kaleidoscopic IFS and hundreds of hybrid formulas. It has lighting, volumetrics, depth of field, keyframe and flight animation, and OpenCL GPU rendering.

## How it works

- Each fractal formula has a **distance estimator**, a function giving a safe distance to the surface. Sphere-tracing (raymarching) steps along rays by that distance until it hits the surface.
- Hybrid fractals alternate formulas per iteration, which gives endless variety.
- The keyframe and flight path tools export frame sequences for film-quality renders.

## Ideas for us

- **synesthetic-room / LED backdrops:** pre-rendered infinite-zoom loops cut to the music.
- **reels-content:** "detail at every scale" fly-through as transition material.
- Copy a formula's distance estimator into a GLSL TOP in TouchDesigner for live, audio-reactive fractals.

entries.license_notes: Code MIT. Demo images and other assets may have separate terms. Voxel renders in the reel were made with MagicaVoxel.
entries.hook: A few rewrite rules can grow mazes, rivers, dungeons and whole voxel buildings.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A probabilistic programming language where programs are XML lists of **rewrite rules** on 2D or 3D grids. Combined, a handful of rules like `RBB=GGR` produce mazes, caves, rivers, dungeons and multi-storey voxel architecture.

## How it works

- A rule `A=B` finds pattern A in the grid and replaces it with B (a Markov algorithm).
- Nodes control application: `one` (apply one random match), `all` (all non-overlapping matches), `prl` (parallel), `sequence` / `markov` (ordering), plus fields, path-finding, convolution and embedded WFC.
- Example `MazeBacktracker`: a red "head" cell carves through black, leaving green corridors, and backtracks when stuck.
- 3D outputs export as `.vox` files for rendering in MagicaVoxel.

## Ideas for us

- **mural-wall:** watching a maze or city *grow* rule by rule is mesmerising. Show the process live, coloured by guest teams.
- **living-floor:** a maze grows under visitors' feet and reroutes around them.
- **reels-content:** voxel building growth timelapses.

## Notes

Sister project to WaveFunctionCollapse (same author). Rules are tiny, so it is easy to port core matching to JS for a web version.

entries.title: Motion Reel ’26 — real motion blur & lens pass in WebGL2
entries.author: SuhaasNv
entries.license_notes: No LICENSE file, so read and learn from it but don't copy code. Default branch is claude/adoring-meitner-fupr6r (a Claude Code working branch), not main.
entries.hook: A 15-second 1080p60 showreel where every frame and every sound is code — real 180° shutter blur, lens warp, grain, numpy score.
entries.source: GitHub guide (opus_motion_video_guide.md)
entries.body:
## What it is

*Motion Reel ’26*: a 15 s, 1080p60 motion-design showreel with no After Effects, stock or samples. It uses a Canvas2D + WebGL2 renderer, a numpy synth and ffmpeg. It works through nine scenes, each showing off a technique:

1. Spring physics with squash and stretch.
2. Kinetic type with an iris match-cut through the "O".
3. A beat-wave grid of shapes.
4. 3,200 closed-form particles (galaxy, Fibonacci sphere, torus knot).
5. An extruded block field.
6. Product-UI motion.
7. GLSL liquid chrome that refracts the type.
8. A 9-cut montage that re-shoots earlier scenes.
9. A seamless loop back to frame 0.

## How it works

- **Pure functions of time:** each scene is `draw(ctx, t)`, so frames render in any order. The montage "re-shoots" earlier moments simply by calling those scenes with an old `t`.
- **Real motion blur:** 8 sub-frames across a 180° shutter per output frame, accumulated in a half-float WebGL2 target and resolved with dither (7,200 sub-frames total).
- **Lens pass** (`src/gl.js`): impact-driven chromatic aberration, barrel warp, flash, vignette, per-frame PCG-hash grain.
- **Camera energy:** one impact envelope drives shake, zoom punch and lens warp, so every hit reads in both picture and sound.
- **On the grid:** 120 BPM; cuts land on beats and exact frame boundaries; the shutter leads each frame so none straddles a cut.
- **Score** (`tools/soundtrack.py`): oscillators and filtered noise only (kicks, claps, sidechained bass, risers, a glass shatter), each placed at its visual event's timestamp.

```bash
python3 tools/soundtrack.py
node tools/render.mjs --workers 4 --samples 8
node tools/render.mjs --stills 2.1,6.5,14.3     # QA stills
```

## Ideas for us

- Apply the sub-frame accumulation trick to TouchDesigner offline renders.
- **rhythm-battle:** one "impact envelope" driving shake, zoom and lens warp on every beat hit.
- Sound placed at visual-event timestamps pairs with our `_shared/sound.ts` procedural audio.

## Notes

Verified 2026-10-03: every technical claim in the guide matches the README. The guide didn't mention that it is a showreel or that there is no license.

## What it is

A production system that coding agents (Claude Code via `CLAUDE.md`, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, Windsurf) drive with natural language to make complete videos: research, script, assets, edit and compose. It mixes code-rendered motion (Remotion, HyperFrames/GSAP) with optional AI generation (Veo, Kling, Runway, FLUX, ...) and free stock archives.

## How it works

- **Three knowledge layers:**
  - Capabilities: `tools/` registry (100+ tools) and `pipeline_defs/` YAML manifests.
  - Methodology: `skills/` Markdown files.
  - Domain knowledge: external documentation packs.
- **12 pipelines:** Animated Explainer, Animation & Motion Graphics, Avatar Spokesperson, Cinematic, Clip Factory, Documentary Montage, Hybrid, Localization & Dub, Podcast Repurposing, Screen Demo, Talking Head, Character Animation.
- **Every pipeline runs the same stages:** `research → proposal → script → scene_plan → assets → edit → compose`.
- **Scored provider selection:** 7 dimensions (task fit, quality, control, reliability, cost, latency, continuity) with an audit trail.
- **Quality gates:** human approvals, pre-compose validation, and post-render self-review (ffprobe, frame sampling, audio silence/clipping checks, subtitle checks).
- **Budget governance:** cost estimate up front, per-action approval threshold ($0.50 default), spend caps.
- **Zero-cost path:** Piper TTS, Pexels/Unsplash/Pixabay/Archive.org/NASA stock, Remotion and FFmpeg.
- **Backlot:** a live production board (`python -m backlot open`).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/calesthio/OpenMontage.git && cd OpenMontage
make setup          # Python 3.10+, Node 18+, FFmpeg required
cp .env.example .env  # all API keys optional
```

## Ideas for us

- **reels-content:** the Clip Factory and Hybrid pipelines could turn raw installation footage into platform-specific cuts (Reels/TikTok/LinkedIn output profiles are built in).
- Steal ideas even without adopting it: the **stage contract** (proposal and scene_plan approvals before spending), the budget gates, and the post-render self-review checklist.
- Pairs with the code-rendered approach: use it to orchestrate, and our own `seek(t)` HTML scenes for brand-exact motion.

## Notes

- AGPL: keep it as an internal tool; don't embed it in client products.
- Demo films in the repo include "The Last Banana" (60 s animated short, reported $1.33 cost).

A Claude Code skill and plugin that works like a film director. It holds five conversations before building anything, then writes the whole film as one JavaScript page and renders it frame by frame with your audio for Reels, TikTok, Shorts, X or YouTube. Example asks: *"Make a 20-second reel of this poem reading: [link]"*, *"An explainer on compound interest with a calm male voiceover (I have an ElevenLabs key)"*, *"A looping visualizer for this track, 16:9, generated music is fine"*.

## How it works

1. **Brief:** it reflects your brief back and measures any reference clip (length, cuts, style).
2. **Sound:** one of four routes: your file, a link via yt-dlp, music and effects generated with Web Audio, or an ElevenLabs/OpenAI voiceover.
3. **Listening:** length, loudness, pauses, sections, tempo and a spectrogram. Whisper aligns any voice, and lyrics or quotes are checked against the canonical text. It then reports "what I hear".
4. **Direction:** look, pacing, 2D or 3D (three.js), what a muted viewer must understand, formats, on-screen text.
5. **Treatment:** logline, central image, palette, and every scene timed to the audio. **Nothing is built until you say go.**

After that it builds, then self-checks:
- a purity test on every frame (`verify.mjs` proves `seek(t)` has no hidden state);
- contact sheets, frame strips, and 1:1 crops of faces and hands.

It renders a master plus an upload copy per platform (lossless frames, correct HD colour, no animated grain so platform re-encodes stay crisp) and gives you an upload checklist.

```
/plugin marketplace add klsoen/opus-js-animations
/plugin install opus-js-animations@opus-js-animations
```

**Requirements:**
- Node ≥ 22 (no `npm install` needed).
- Chrome or Chromium (`CHROME=/path`).
- ffmpeg.
- Python 3 + numpy, plus `openai-whisper` for voice alignment.
- yt-dlp (fetched automatically).
- Optional ElevenLabs/OpenAI key, read from the environment or `~/.config/opus-js-animations/keys.env`, never written into the project.

## Ideas for us

- The fastest path to trying the technique on a real CTX reel. Install it, then feed it installation footage audio.
- Read `references/` even without installing it:
  - `delivery.md`: why some Instagram uploads look sharp.
  - `styles.md`: a style menu.
  - `tiles-and-flocks.md`: WebGL2 instancing for thousands of elements, relevant to memory-mosaic and living-swarm.
  - `production.md`: minutes-long films with parallel agents.

## Notes

Verified 2026-10-03: README and the full `skills/opus-js-animations/` tree (SKILL.md, 13 reference docs, render/stills/verify scripts, `film-template.html`) match the guide. Young project (created 2026-09-24, few stars), so review `SKILL.md` before installing.

## What it is

Each skill teaches Opus 5.5 to make a whole video in one style, covering storyboard, animation, review, music and encode. All imagery and music are procedural code; frames are pure functions of time, rendered in headless Chrome and encoded with ffmpeg.
- **painted-animation:** p5.js + p5.brush watercolour and ink cartoon with an expression and acting library. Music videos are cut to the measured beat, and lyric videos get word-by-word karaoke subtitles.
- **kinetic-reel:** condensed display type plus HUD micro-type over three.js layers (particle terrain, liquid marble, chrome knot, a particle cloud that condenses into a shape), with shape-continuity transitions and a score synthesised from the same timeline.

## How it works

```
/plugin marketplace add tuzhechen2005/opus-video-skills
/plugin install painted-animation@opus-video-skills
/plugin install kinetic-reel@opus-video-skills
```
Then, for example: "Make a 60-second kinetic-type reel of my three projects from this résumé." Requires Node, Chrome and ffmpeg (and Python + numpy for tempo detection).

## Ideas for us

- **kinetic-reel** is close to a CTX portfolio/showreel out of the box: feed it our installation list.
- Its "new style = new skill folder + template + example" contract is a good pattern for a CTX house-style skill.

## Notes

entries.title: Origami Simulator — paper folding in the browser
entries.author: Amanda Ghassaei
entries.license_notes: Code MIT. Individual crease patterns and media have their own terms; real-paper foldability not guaranteed.
entries.hook: A flat sheet of paper folds itself into a crane, right in the browser.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A WebGL app that loads a crease pattern (SVG or FOLD) and simulates the sheet folding up. A slider controls the fold percentage, and a strain heatmap shows where the paper would stretch. Results export as STL, OBJ or FOLD.

## How it works

Based on Ghassaei, Demaine & Gershenfeld, *Fast, Interactive Origami Simulation using GPU Computation* (OSME 2018):

- The sheet is a triangle mesh with **axial (bar) constraints** to keep edge lengths, **crease constraints** (torsional springs that drive the dihedral angle towards target fold × percentage), and **face constraints** to keep triangles from shearing.
- All constraints are solved in parallel on the GPU every frame, so even complex patterns fold in real time.

## Ideas for us

- **Brand reveal:** a flat logo sheet folds into a 3D mark on the big screen.
- **mural-wall:** a guest's drawing is texture-mapped onto the sheet, then folds into a crane that flies into a flock.
- **reels-content:** the fold animation as a transition.
- Export STL for printable keepsakes.

## Notes

The crease-pattern library is large; check the terms of each pattern before using it commercially.

entries.title: Paper-cut animation — how to get the cut-paper / diorama look in code
entries.author: Synthesis of the repos linked below
entries.hook: Layered cardstock shapes with contact shadows, ragged cut edges, paper grain, held frames and paper-wipe cuts — a style code (or a video model) can hit reliably.
entries.source: User request, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

Cut-paper animation looks like coloured paper shapes stacked in layers and moved under a camera, like stop-motion or a lit diorama. It's popular in reels, explainers and myth or folklore shorts, and has deep roots in Chinese paper-cutting (剪纸), Japanese kirie (切り絵) and Lotte Reiniger's silhouette films. It suits code well because every element is a flat shape.

## How it works

**Ingredients (each one is cheap):**
1. **Flat shapes, few colours:** a strict 3–5 colour palette, no gradients inside shapes (cardstock-diorama-myth enforces exactly three).
2. **Cut edges:** offset each path's outline with low-frequency noise so edges look scissored; add a 1–2 px lighter "core" edge where paper thickness shows.
3. **Depth = layers:** 4–8 planes with **soft contact shadows** (a blurred, offset, darkened copy of each layer onto the one below). Move the layers at different speeds for parallax, which reads as a diorama.
4. **Paper grain:** multiply a fibre texture or noise per layer; for print looks add **riso / halftone** (overprint multiply, misregistration, ink mottling) in a shader, as animation-pipeline does.
5. **Stop-motion timing:** hold poses "on twos" (12 fps steps inside a 24/30 fps film) and add tiny per-frame jitter in position and rotation. Smooth eases look wrong here.
6. **Transitions:** a paper sheet sliding over the frame (the "paper wipe") or a fold or tear. These also hide every cut.
7. **Lighting:** for "paper lightbox" scenes, light comes *through* the paper (backlit knockouts, glowing cut windows).
8. **Sound:** paper foley (rustle, slide, snip) sells it.

**Routes:**
- **Pure code:** opus-js-animations (its `styles.md` lists cut-paper stop-motion and paper lightbox; its *Shaml* demo is a medallion of 336 cut-paper pieces) or animation-pipeline (riso cut-paper shader).
- **Code + generated sprites:** vox-editorial (cut paper with scissored subjects, Python + ffmpeg) or vox-skill (paper collage in Remotion).
- **Generative video:** cardstock-diorama-myth (style key + Seedance clips + paper wipes).
- **No-code:** DistilBook's "cut paper collage" style, or the HyperFrames `vox-explainer` collage skill.
- **Hand animation:** OpenToonz plastic/cut-out rigging.

## Ideas for us

- **mural-wall:** guests' drawings are cut out (segmentation), given a paper edge and contact shadow, and dropped into a layered paper diorama that slowly parallaxes.
- **reels-content:** a CTX "paper" house style is cheap to keep consistent across many reels.
- **synesthetic-room:** a projected paper lightbox where crowd energy lights cut windows.

## Notes

Built from the READMEs of the linked repos (read 2026-10-03). Low-star paper-cut repos found but not added: Airpyk-98/epic-paper-cutout-animation (prompt system), cameronha/paper-collage-animation (Gemini + ffmpeg).

entries.source: GitHub guide (opus_motion_video_guide.md)
entries.body:
## What it is

The source for the music video *I'm Upping My P(doom)*. Claude Opus 5.5 made it in Claude Code in two generations, and every file in the repo was written by the model. The only human direction was "use the Clawd character" and "give each lyric interesting visuals and transitions". Created 2026-09-22; about 1.7k stars when checked.

## How it works

- `studio.html`: the page every frame is painted in, with p5.js + p5.brush.
- `src/ch/c01_lab.js` … `c09_finale.js`: nine chapter files, one per section of the song.
- `src/`: shared code (`clawd.js`, `cast.js`, `props.js`, `lyrics.js`, `timeline.js`, `core.js`).
- `STORYBOARD.md`: Opus's shot-by-shot plan, written after the first generation once it was told to use brush strokes and make every scene transition into the next.
- `ANIMATION_GUIDE.md`: the style and code brief Opus wrote for the sub-agents it ran in parallel.
- `legacy/`: the first generation (Opus 5.5 at Medium effort), kept for comparison.
- `render.mjs`: paints frames in headless Chrome (resumable), then muxes in `assets/pdoom.mp3` with ffmpeg.

```bash
npm install
node render.mjs --frames=0:156.6 --workers=4   # → out/frames (resumable)
node render.mjs --encode --out=out/pdoom.mp4
```

Needs Node, Google Chrome and ffmpeg; pass `--chrome=<path>` if Chrome isn't in the default location.

## Ideas for us

- Copy the **STORYBOARD.md + ANIMATION_GUIDE.md** pattern for any multi-scene piece. The guide is what keeps parallel sub-agents visually consistent.
- Compare `legacy/` with the final version to see what the second pass (storyboard first, brush medium, forced transitions) improved.

## Notes

Verified 2026-10-03 against the README and file tree at the pinned commit. Everything the guide described is present, including the nine `src/ch/` files.

entries.author: Luisma Peramato (PeramatoG)

entries.source: Research for stage design / rigging request, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

A desktop app for viewing, editing and exporting MVR stage files with GDTF fixture libraries. It shows a 3D view plus plan-focused 2D workflows for reviewing fixtures, **trusses, hoists**, objects and scene structure. It is deliberately *not* a real-time DMX visualiser.

## How it works

- Import/export MVR; maintain a personal GDTF library; fetch profiles from the GDTF Share API (free account).
- **Tools → Create from text:** generates elements from rider-style notes.
- Create, modify and distribute MVR elements from the **command line**, which makes it scriptable by an agent.
- Linux AppImage, Windows and macOS builds in Releases.

## Ideas for us

- A quick check of a lighting designer's rig before an event; produce 2D truss and hoist plans for riggers from the same MVR.
- Its "create from text" and CLI pair well with Claude: describe a stage → MVR draft.

## Notes

README read 2026-10-03. Actively developed (about 117 stars).

entries.title: primitive — images rebuilt from simple shapes
entries.author: Michael Fogleman
entries.license_notes: Input masterpieces in the reel were public domain.
entries.hook: It repaints any picture using only simple shapes, added one at a time.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A CLI that approximates an image with N geometric primitives (triangles, rectangles, ellipses, circles, rotated rects, Bézier curves, polygons). It outputs PNG, SVG, or a GIF of the build-up.

## How it works

1. Start with a canvas filled with the image's average colour.
2. For each new shape: try random candidates, then **hill-climb** (mutate position, size and angle) to minimise RMSE between the canvas and the target. The best shape's colour is solved analytically.
3. Add the winner, then repeat. Each shape is the single best improvement available.

`primitive -i in.png -o out.svg -n 200 -m 1` (m: 0 combo, 1 triangle, 2 rect, 3 ellipse, 4 circle, 5 rotated rect, 6 beziers, 7 rotated ellipse, 8 polygon).

## Ideas for us

- **memory-mosaic alternative:** the wall rebuilds the target image shape by shape live, one shape per guest submission.
- **merch-takeaway:** a guest selfie turned into a 150-triangle poster; Bézier mode plotted with a pen.
- **reels-content:** the build-up GIF is satisfying content on its own.

## Notes

Browser ports exist (e.g. primitive.js); it is easy to reimplement with WebGL for scoring candidates.

entries.author: The Ready Bunch (GollyGang)

entries.hook: Stripes, spots and snowflakes growing out of equations.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A desktop program (with the `rdy` command-line tool) for exploring reaction-diffusion and other continuous cellular automata on 2D/3D grids and meshes, GPU-accelerated with OpenCL. It ships with a large library of named patterns. The reel's footage is simulation output computed with `rdy`, not screen recordings.

## How it works

The Gray-Scott model has two chemicals, A and B, on a grid:

```
dA/dt = Da·∇²A − A·B² + f·(1 − A)
dB/dt = Db·∇²B + A·B² − (k + f)·B
```

Small changes in feed `f` and kill `k` switch the result between spots, stripes, mazes, mitosis and coral. Ready lets you tune these live and also supports other formulas (Brusselator, FitzHugh–Nagumo, ...).

## Ideas for us

- **living-floor:** footsteps inject chemical B, so trails bloom into coral or leopard patterns that persist and evolve.
- TouchDesigner: two-texture GLSL feedback loop, which is trivial to implement. Use Ready to *find* good f/k values, then hard-code them.
- **mural-wall:** guests' drawings used as the seed mask.

## Notes

GPL: don't paste its code into client deliverables. The equations themselves are free to implement.

entries.title: RVO2 — ORCA collision avoidance for crowds
entries.author: Jur van den Berg, Stephen J. Guy, Jamie Snape, Ming C. Lin, Dinesh Manocha — UNC Chapel Hill
entries.license_notes: Code Apache-2.0. README excerpts in the reel were UNC, CC BY-SA 4.0.
entries.hook: 250 agents cross a circle at the same time and nobody collides.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A reference implementation of ORCA, the standard algorithm for many agents moving to goals without colliding. The classic demo puts 250 agents on a circle and sends each to the opposite side; they swirl through the centre without touching.

## How it works

- Every agent has a position, radius, max speed and a **preferred velocity** (straight to its goal).
- For each nearby neighbour, ORCA builds a **half-plane of allowed velocities** that guarantees no collision within a time horizon τ, with each agent taking *half* the responsibility (reciprocity, which prevents oscillation).
- Each agent solves a tiny 2D linear program: the velocity closest to its preferred velocity that satisfies all the half-planes. If none is feasible, it takes the least-bad one.
- A k-d tree finds neighbours, so it scales to thousands of agents.

## Ideas for us

- **living-swarm:** creatures that flow around visitors (visitors become static or slow ORCA obstacles) and never clip through each other.
- **memory-mosaic alternative reveal:** each guest becomes a coloured agent whose goal is a pixel of the target image. The crowd assembles the picture without overlaps (the post's own question: give each agent a colour and destination).
- **living-floor:** avoid-the-feet particles.

## Notes

- Ports: RVO2-3D (C++), Python-RVO2 (Cython), RVO2-CS (C#/Unity), several JS ports. The core is small enough to port to a GLSL/compute pass with a grid neighbour search.

entries.title: SceneFlow — script-to-screen sync for AI filmmakers
entries.author: Taruma Sakti Megariansyah (taruma)
entries.hook: Plays a video alongside its script and lights up each line — dialogue, camera, VFX, transitions — as it appears, to judge whether AI footage followed the prompt.
entries.source: User shared names, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

A browser tool that syncs a screenplay (or its structured "Auteur Script" format with 5-part staging metadata) to a video and highlights in real time which instructions are on screen. It's built to evaluate prompt adherence in AI-generated video: missed elements, camera drift, continuity breaks.

## How it works

- **Cues** link script segments to timestamps, in 8 colour-coded types: dialogue, action, camera, shot, audio, VFX, transition, environment. There is a colour-blind-safe palette mode.
- Cues are written by hand in a 3-panel edit workstation, or generated with a multimodal model. It ships a ready Gemini sync prompt and a JSON schema for one-click structured cue generation.
- The display is a multi-track DAW-style timeline with a smooth rAF-driven clock and a playhead fixed at 35% so upcoming cues are visible. Nudges of ±0.1 s / ±0.5 s, loop previews, and per-type timing buffers.
- Projects are portable JSON (versionable). The source video is a YouTube link.

## Ideas for us

- **QA for generated or code-rendered reels:** write the storyboard as an Auteur Script, then check the render against it shot by shot. It works for our `STORYBOARD.md`-style pipelines too.
- Client review: show a client the script and the cut side by side.

## Notes

README read 2026-10-03. "SceneFlow" is also a computer-vision term (3D motion estimation); this entry is the filmmaking tool.

entries.license_notes: Paintings referenced in the reel (Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains) are public domain via Wikimedia Commons.
entries.hook: An endless Chinese landscape scroll painted entirely by code.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A procedurally generated, infinitely scrolling *shan shui* (mountain-water) ink landscape in the browser, drawn as SVG. It was inspired by Song-dynasty hand scrolls.

## How it works

- Terrain silhouettes come from layered Perlin noise. Each mountain is built from strokes, texture dabs (cun) and shading washes.
- Trees, pavilions, boats, bridges and tiny figures are separate procedural generators placed along the terrain.
- The canvas is generated in chunks as you scroll, so it never ends, and a seed in the URL reproduces a scroll.

## Ideas for us

- **mural-wall:** a long projected scroll that slowly pans all night, seeded with the event name. Guests' drawings could be tucked in as tiny figures in the landscape.
- **synesthetic-room:** calm state = ink scroll; louder crowd = more mist and wind.
- An aesthetic reference: it shows how far "stroke-based" procedural drawing can go.

## Notes

Pure SVG DOM, so for huge walls you might rasterise chunks to canvas for performance.

entries.title: Shape Shifter — SVG path-morphing icon animation tool
entries.author: Alex Lockwood
entries.hook: Morph one SVG shape into another cleanly — it makes two paths "compatible" (same points and commands) and exports SVG, spritesheets or Android animations.
entries.source: User shared name, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

A web app (about 4k stars, actively maintained, created 2016) for building icon animations, especially **path morphs** (play to pause, menu to back arrow, logo to logo). It exports standalone SVGs, SVG spritesheets, and Android `AnimatedVectorDrawable`.

## How it works

To morph shape A into shape B, both SVG paths must have the **same number and type of drawing commands** in a matching order. Design tools hide this, so Shape Shifter lets you:
- add or remove points without changing a path's look, and drag them along the path;
- reverse or shift the start point and split subpaths so the points pair up sensibly;
- auto-fix paths to be compatible, then preview the in-between states on a timeline;
- convert unsupported primitives (circles, etc.) into curve commands.

The same logic underlies GSAP MorphSVG and flubber-style interpolation.

## Ideas for us

- Brand logo morphs for event intros and reels (client logo → CTX mark → event title).
- Morphing icons in our phone-side join and conduct UIs.
- **mural-wall:** morph a guest's simplified doodle outline into a target shape.

entries.source: GitHub guide (opus_motion_video_guide.md)
entries.body:
## What it is

A live product (launchvideo.io). One OpenComputer agent called `director`, running Claude Opus 5.5, writes a single 1920×1080 HTML film from a URL or a prompt, renders it, and hands back an MP4. It has a one-click deploy to your own OpenComputer account.

## How it works

1. `POST /api/jobs` creates an OpenComputer session and sends a `JOB` block.
2. In URL mode, the agent's `web_fetch` tool also extracts the page title, headings, **most-used hex colours and Google Fonts** for the brand look.
3. The agent writes the film (CSS keyframes or a rAF loop), then runs `check_scene`, which loads it under the virtual clock and reports JS errors and visible text at several timestamps. It fixes what it finds, then calls `render_video`.
4. `render_video` uses Playwright's headless shell with an **injected virtual clock**: rAF, timers, `Date` and CSS/WAAPI animations are all driven by `__seek(t)`. JPEG frames are piped to ffmpeg (`libx264`, `crf 18`, `yuv420p`, `faststart`).
5. The MP4 is saved to the session workspace (`/workspace/videos/<job>.mp4`), and the web app signs a download link.

A 30 s film renders in about 30–40 s. The first call in each fresh microVM spends about a minute installing Chromium and ffmpeg.

**Determinism rules:** no `<video>`, `<audio>` or `<iframe>`, no CSS transitions, no `Math.random`, no external images in a scene.

## Ideas for us

- The **virtual-clock injection** is the key trick. It could record our existing React installation clients frame-perfect without rewriting them as `draw(t)`.
- The `check_scene` step (load the scene, read the errors and visible text at sample times) is a cheap self-QA pattern for any agent-written animation.
- Brand extraction from a URL (colours and fonts) gives instant on-brand client teasers.

## Notes

Verified 2026-10-03 against the README and file tree. **Correction to the guide:** finished videos are not uploaded to Vercel Blob. They stay in the OpenComputer session workspace and are served by signed download ("no object storage"). Vercel only hosts the web form.

5. The MP4 is saved to the session workspace (`/workspace/videos/<job>.mp4`), and the web app signs a download link.

A 30 s film renders in about 30–40 s. The first call in each fresh microVM spends about a minute installing Chromium and ffmpeg.

**Determinism rules:** no `<video>`, `<audio>` or `<iframe>`, no CSS transitions, no `Math.random`, no external images in a scene.
sections.Ideas for us:
- The **virtual-clock injection** is the key trick. It could record our existing React installation clients frame-perfect without rewriting them as `draw(t)`.
- The `check_scene` step (load the scene, read the errors and visible text at sample times) is a cheap self-QA pattern for any agent-written animation.
- Brand extraction from a URL (colours and fonts) gives instant on-brand client teasers.

entries.title: Stage design, truss & rigging — workflow, tools and safety
entries.author: Synthesis (industry practice)
entries.license_notes: Commercial tools named here are paid; manufacturer CAD libraries are free downloads with their own terms.
entries.hook: How an event stage goes from concept to safe rig: 3D design with manufacturer truss models → MVR → lighting previz → rigging plot and load sign-off by a qualified rigger.
entries.source: Research for stage design / rigging request, 2026-10-03
entries.body:
## What it is

A map of the stage-design toolchain and the part that must not be improvised: truss and rigging loads.

## How it works

**1. Concept and 3D design.** Model the venue, stage, set and screens. Use free 3D/CAD models and load tables from truss makers (Prolyte, Global Truss, Eurotruss, Tomcat, Area Four Industries...) so dimensions and allowable loads are real.
- **Industry tools (paid):** Vectorworks Spotlight (CAD + rigging plots), Capture, Depence, WYSIWYG, grandMA3 3D; Unreal Engine for high-end previz and virtual production.
- **Free/open:** Blender (+ BlenderDMX, + Blender MCP), Perastage for MVR review.

**2. Interchange.** Export the rig as **MVR** with GDTF fixtures, so the lighting desk, visualiser and content team (TouchDesigner via td-gdtf) all share one rig.

**3. Rigging plot.** Hang points, motor/hoist positions and capacities, truss spans and types, bridles, and point loads (fixtures + cable + screens + dynamic factors). Perastage shows trusses and hoists from MVR, and Vectorworks Spotlight produces formal plots.

**4. Load calculation and sign-off.** Truss load tables give allowable uniformly-distributed and point loads per span. Hoists need rated working-load limits plus a safety factor. Roof or ceiling points need venue structural approval. **This must be done or checked by a competent rigger or structural engineer.** Relevant standards include ANSI E1.2 (aluminium truss and towers), EN 17206 (stage machinery safety), and local regulations.

## Ideas for us

- For CTX installations that hang screens, projectors or sensors: model them on manufacturer truss in Blender, export MVR, review in Perastage, and hand the plot to the venue's rigger.
- Previz content plus lights plus truss in one scene for pitches (BlenderDMX renders, Virtual Mapper for projection).
- Let Claude draft the layout (Blender MCP / Perastage CLI). **Never** let an AI or an unreviewed calculator decide loads.

## Notes

Written from general industry knowledge (2026-10-03) and not verified per tool. Open-source truss load calculators on GitHub are tiny unreviewed projects (0–1 stars) and are deliberately not listed as tools.

entries.title: Taichi — GPU physics in ~100 lines of Python (MPM)
entries.author: Yuanming Hu & the Taichi community
entries.license_notes: The README code illustration (fractal_code.png) has separate image terms, not confirmed.
entries.hook: Water, jelly and snow colliding — from about a hundred lines of Python on the GPU.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A Python-embedded language that JIT-compiles kernels to CUDA, Vulkan or Metal. Its famous examples, `mpm88.py`, `mpm99.py` and `mpm128.py` (shown in the reel, about 122 lines of code), simulate water, elastic jelly and snow interacting, using the Material Point Method.

## How it works

MLS-MPM loop each substep:

1. **P2G:** particles scatter mass and momentum (plus stress from their deformation gradient) to a background grid.
2. **Grid update:** divide by mass to get velocity, add gravity, apply boundary conditions.
3. **G2P:** particles gather the new velocity and an affine field (APIC), then update position and deformation gradient. Snow plasticity clamps the singular values.

Taichi's `@ti.kernel` makes the per-particle and per-cell loops run in parallel on the GPU automatically.

## Ideas for us

- **living-floor:** a sand or snow field that guests' tracked feet push around (Taichi sidecar → Spout/NDI or shared texture into TouchDesigner).
- **reels-content:** offline high-res renders of crowd-coloured materials colliding.
- Rapid prototyping of any custom simulation before porting to GLSL.

## Notes

- `pip install taichi`, then `ti example mpm128`.
- Yuanming Hu's GAMES 201 course notes: https://yuanming.taichi.graphics/

entries.title: TAPNet / TAPIR / TAPNext — track any point in video
entries.author: Google DeepMind
entries.license_notes: Apache-2.0 for code and linked pretrained checkpoints. Footage in the reel was CC0 (Wikimedia Commons).
entries.hook: Pick any pixel in a video and it follows that exact point to the end — even through occlusion.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

DeepMind's repo for the "Tracking Any Point" family: the TAP-Vid benchmark plus the TAPIR, BootsTAP and TAPNext trackers. The reel features the newest tracker, TAPNext++. You give it query points (x, y, frame) and it returns each point's trajectory and visibility in every frame.

## How it works

- **TAPIR:** per-frame matching of the query feature against every frame to get a rough track, then iterative temporal refinement using local correlations. Online (causal) variants exist for live streams.
- **TAPNext:** treats tracking as next-token prediction over video frames, which keeps it causal and lets it run frame by frame.
- Outputs are per-point (x, y) tracks plus an occlusion flag, so you can draw trails, dot grids or attach graphics.

## Ideas for us

- **reels-content:** "data-viz on footage" overlays: dense rainbow dot grids that ride on a dancer, horse or crowd (the cheetah and octopus shots in the reel).
- Track points on event footage to pin labels or particles onto performers in post, without manual rotoscoping.
- Possible live use: an online TAPIR on a GPU box sends tracks to TouchDesigner over OSC. Check latency first.

## Notes

- GPU recommended; Colab notebooks are in the repo.
- Credit the footage separately from the code (the reel credits each Wikimedia clip).

entries.body:
## What it is

The companion code to Matthias Müller's *Ten Minute Physics* YouTube channel (he co-invented Position Based Dynamics). Each lesson is a standalone `NN-topic.html`, including interaction, XPBD, soft bodies, cloth (`14-cloth.html`), self-collision with spatial hashing, Eulerian and FLIP fluids, and more. Each has a PDF of the slides.

## How it works

- **XPBD:** predict positions from velocity, then repeatedly project constraints (distance, volume, bending) directly on positions, with a compliance term so stiffness doesn't depend on iteration count. Velocity = Δposition / dt.
- Spatial hashing gives cheap neighbour queries for collisions.
- Everything is plain JS with three.js for display, so it is easy to read and port.

## Ideas for us

- **digital-doodles-wall / mural-wall:** a cloth curtain or soft-body blobs that guests poke and drag from their phones.
- **rhythm-battle:** bass hits drive impulses into a soft-body mesh.
- The cleanest reference for porting physics into TouchDesigner GLSL or compute shaders.

## Notes

Demos run straight from the GitHub Pages link, with no build step. Great teaching material for new team members.

entries.title: Three Ways of Generating Terrain with Erosion
entries.author: Daniel Andrino
entries.license_notes: Code MIT. Elevation maps from USGS (credited in the original project). ML examples by the author.
entries.hook: Realistic eroded landscapes three ways — simulate water, learn from real elevation data, or grow river networks.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A well-written comparison of three ways to make heightmaps that *look eroded*, with Python code and rendered shaded-relief images for each.

## How it works

1. **Simulation:** start from noise, then run a grid-based hydraulic erosion loop. Rain adds water, water flows downhill, picks up sediment where it is fast and drops it where it slows, and evaporates. The reel shows the simulation converging ("iteration 716 / 716").
2. **Machine learning:** a GAN trained on real USGS elevation tiles generates new terrain that already has erosion features.
3. **River networks:** generate a drainage network first, then derive the terrain heights from it, so the valleys are correct by construction.

Each output is rendered as a hillshaded map with hypsometric tints (water blue, green lowlands, white peaks).

## Ideas for us

- **living-floor:** a projected topographic island; footsteps add rain locally so visitors literally erode the land over the night.
- TouchDesigner sand / ecosystem builds: port the hydraulic step to GLSL feedback TOPs (height + water + sediment in RGBA).
- Contour-line version of the heightmap for plotter merch.

## Notes

The simulation code is plain NumPy, so it is easy to port to GLSL or Taichi for real-time use.

entries.title: TileableVolumeNoise — 3D noise for volumetric clouds
entries.author: Sébastien Hillaire (with weirdfoo)
entries.license_notes: Worley function credited to Marc-Andre Loyer in code. The cloud raymarcher in the reel was by Xity, not part of the repo.
aliases: Physically Based Sky Atmosphere and Cloud Rendering
entries.hook: The noise textures behind Frostbite's sky and cloud talk — tileable 3D noise you raymarch into clouds.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A small C++ collection of functions that generate **tileable** 3D noise volumes (Perlin, Worley/cellular, and Perlin-Worley). It is the code from the Frostbite team's SIGGRAPH 2016 talk *Physically Based Sky, Atmosphere and Cloud Rendering in Frostbite*.

## How it works

- **Tileable:** the noise wraps at the volume borders, so a 128³ texture repeats seamlessly across the sky.
- **Shape texture (≈128³ RGBA):** R = Perlin-Worley (billowy, connected), G/B/A = Worley FBM at increasing frequencies.
- **Detail texture (≈32³):** higher-frequency Worley that erodes the cloud edges.
- At render time, a raymarcher samples density = remap(shape, detail erosion, coverage and height gradient), then applies Beer-Lambert absorption plus a phase function for silver linings. This is the same recipe as Guerrilla's Horizon Zero Dawn clouds.

## Ideas for us

- **synesthetic-room:** a raymarched cloud ceiling; crowd energy raises coverage and storminess, and quiet thins it to wisps.
- TouchDesigner: bake the volumes once to a 3D texture (Texture 3D TOP), then raymarch in a GLSL TOP.
- Slow-motion cloud plates for reels.

## Notes

Generate offline (C++), save as a texture, then load it anywhere. The generation step doesn't need to run live.

entries.title: vpype — Swiss-army knife for plotter vector graphics
entries.author: Antoine Beyeler & contributors
entries.hook: One CLI pipeline to read, clean, optimise and lay out any SVG for a pen plotter.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

A command-line pipeline for plotter-ready vector graphics. You chain commands in one line, for example `vpype read in.svg linemerge linesort reloop linesimplify layout a4 write out.svg`.

## How it works

- Commands operate on layers of polylines: `read`, `linemerge` (join touching lines), `linesort` (shortest pen-up travel), `linesimplify`, `reloop`, `splitall`, `layout` / `scale` / `rotate`, `write` (SVG or HPGL).
- A plugin system adds generators and effects; `vsketch` is the companion sketching framework.
- A viewer (`show`) previews the result, including pen-up travel.

## Ideas for us

- **merch-takeaway:** the last step for any generated line art (ln, stippling, fishdraw, differential-line) before an AxiDraw prints a guest's take-home.
- Cut plot time at live events: `linesort` often halves the drawing time.

## Notes

`pip install vpype[all]`.

entries.title: WaveFunctionCollapse — grow images from a tiny example
entries.author: Maxim Gumin (mxgmn)
entries.license_notes: Code MIT. Input samples, tiles and README art by Maxim Gumin are OUTSIDE the MIT license — make our own tiles.
entries.hook: From one tiny example image, it grows a whole new picture that follows the same local rules.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

The algorithm that generates new bitmaps or tile maps that look locally like a small input sample. It is used in Townscaper-style towns, Bad North, Caves of Qud and countless level generators.

## How it works

1. **Learn:** *overlapping model*: cut every N×N pattern from the sample and record frequencies and which patterns may overlap. *Simple tiled model*: use given tiles plus adjacency rules.
2. **Wave:** every output cell starts as a superposition of all patterns.
3. **Observe:** pick the cell with the lowest Shannon entropy and collapse it to one pattern, weighted by frequency.
4. **Propagate:** remove now-impossible patterns from neighbours, rippling outwards (arc consistency).
5. Repeat until everything is collapsed. On contradiction, restart (or backtrack).

## Ideas for us

- **mural-wall / digital-doodles-wall:** a guest draws a tiny 8×8 pixel sample on their phone, and the wall grows a whole tapestry from it.
- Generative tile backgrounds that change per event but stay on-brand (feed it brand-colour samples).
- **memory-mosaic:** layout constraints for non-grid mosaics.

## Notes

The visual "collapse" process (low-entropy cells resolving first) is beautiful to show live, not just the result. JS ports exist (e.g. kchapelier/wavefunctioncollapse).

entries.title: WebGL Fluid Simulation — live swirling dye
entries.author: Pavel Dobryakov (PavelDoGreat)
entries.license_notes: The App Store app shown in the reel is a separate commercial product with separate image terms.
entries.hook: Every swirl is calculated live in the browser — draw a stroke and the colour flows.
entries.source: Instagram @index.opensource (curated by @hyun2xyz)
entries.body:
## What it is

The famous single-page GPU fluid toy: drag across the screen and coloured dye swirls with vorticity, bloom and sun rays. It runs on phones too.

## How it works

Jos Stam's *Stable Fluids* on framebuffers, per frame:

1. **Splat:** pointer strokes add velocity and dye (gaussian splats).
2. **Advect:** dye and velocity are moved along the velocity field (semi-Lagrangian).
3. **Curl + vorticity confinement:** re-injects small swirls.
4. **Divergence → pressure (Jacobi iterations) → subtract gradient:** makes the flow incompressible.
5. **Display:** shading, bloom and sunrays post passes.

Config knobs: `SIM_RESOLUTION`, `DYE_RESOLUTION`, `DENSITY_DISSIPATION`, `VELOCITY_DISSIPATION`, `PRESSURE`, `PRESSURE_ITERATIONS`, `CURL`, `SPLAT_RADIUS`, `SPLAT_FORCE`, `SHADING`, `COLORFUL`, `BLOOM`, `SUNRAYS`.

## Ideas for us

- **digital-doodles-wall:** phone swipes inject dye into the shared wall.
- **rhythm-battle:** beats trigger splats; each team has its own colour; the dominant colour wins.
- **synesthetic-room:** crowd volume → `CURL` and splat force; quiet = high dissipation and calm.
- Drop-in background for any web installation (MIT, single file).

## Notes

The post's tuning order: (1) draw strokes → (2) colour moves with velocity → (3) pressure solve → (4) vorticity and lighting settings for mood.
